title: Multicellular signaling in reverse cardiac remodeling revealed by integrated bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics
summary: Heart failure results from maladaptive multicellular remodeling triggered by sustained biomechanical stress. Although mechanical unloading can promote reverse remodeling, recovery is frequently incomplete and its mechanistic basis remains unclear. Using a reversible murine pressure-overload model combined with bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics, we demonstrate that reverse remodeling represents an actively maintained yet constrained multicellular state. Unloading improved cardiac function and partially restored extracellular matrix and metabolic programs, whereas inflammatory and mitochondrial dysfunction signatures persisted. Cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells largely re-established homeostatic transcriptional states, while fibroblasts retained activated programs that dominated residual pathology. Multicellular factor analysis delineated a reversible metabolic stress program and a persistent inflammatory-mitochondrial program coordinated across cardiac cell types. Cell-cell communication analysis identified lymphatic endothelial cells as key instructive regulators of recovery. Notably, lymphatic-derived Reelin (RELN) directly suppressed pathological fetal gene activation in murine and human cardiomyocytes, uncovering a previously unrecognized lymphoangiocrine mechanism that constrains myocardial recovery in chronic heart failure.

title: The bile acid receptor TGR5 is a modulator of the bone marrow microenvironment
summary: The gut is an emerging regulator of bone marrow (BM) hematopoiesis, with several molecules involved in this communication. Among them, bile acids (BAs) act as a relay between the microbiota and the rest of the body by activating specific receptors, including Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5). Although TGR5 has potent regulatory effects in immune cells, its role in the BM remains unclear. Here, we show that TGR5 is expressed across hematopoietic populations, including hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. While TGR5 deficiency did not affect steady-state hematopoiesis, it mildly impaired cell-autonomous short-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, TGR5 deletion altered the BM microenvironment. Young male, but not female, Tgr5-/- mice showed reduced bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) alongside an accumulation of BM adipocyte progenitors, consistent with impaired progenitor differentiation. TGR5 deficiency also blunted BMAT expansion during obesity and aging, with reduced myeloid-lymphoid progenitor ratios in male mice. Together, our results indicate that TGR5 contributes to sex-dependent regulation of BM adiposity and identify it as a potential target for modulating the BM niche.

title: Activation of perivascular thermogenic fat improves aortic stenosis
summary: Aim: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a common condition with exponential increases in incidence in aging populations. Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) forms the outer layer of the aortic wall and has - especially in the thoracic area - characteristics of thermogenic adipose tissue, which dissipates energy and releases endocrine factors. Here, we set out to investigate the role of thermogenic PVAT in AS. Methods and results: We studied the role of (PVAT) in the development of AS in a murine model of AS. To specifically delineate the role of PVAT activity in AS, we used a pharmacological {beta}3-adrenergic agonist as well as cold exposure in combination with a genetic mouse model with deficient PVAT development. To investigate the role of thermogenic adipose tissue in human AS, we used 18F-FDG PET-CT imaging. We found that pharmacological activation of thermogenic adipose tissue resulted in an improvement of AS, but not in mice genetically deficient in PVAT. Similarly, PVAT was found to be protective against AS during physiological stimulation of PVAT using cold exposure. Mechanistically, PVAT activation resulted in enhanced aortic distensibility and cellular remodeling of the aortic wall, possibly via release of polyunsaturated fatty acids and oxylipins from perivascular adipocytes. Finally, analysis of thermogenic fat activity in humans revealed that mediastinal thermogenic fat activity correlated negatively with diagnostic criteria of AS severity, suggesting an important role for PVAT activity in human AS. Conclusion: Our data indicate that PVAT activation reduces aortic stenosis and supports aortic remodeling to improve ascending aorta hemodynamics. PVAT activation might be a novel therapeutic target to ameliorate AS progression. Translational perspective: Currently, there are no effective strategies for treating AS other than valve replacement. Since the molecular mechanisms underlying the disease progression remain unclear, there are no pharmacological agents approved for either treatment or prevention of this disease. Furthermore, AS development cannot currently be predicted and is often only diagnosed when patients develop symptoms, which may be 10-20 years after disease onset. Therefore, identifying novel mechanisms that improve aortic valve function and prevent AS is of high medical need. This study identifies activation of PVAT-dependent aortic remodeling as a potential new therapeutic approach to improve or prevent AS.
